{{Short description|Graph of a dynamical system}}
In mathematics, a '''Bratteli diagram''' is a combinatorial structure: a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] composed of vertices labelled by positive integers ("level") and unoriented edges between vertices having levels differing by one.  The notion was introduced by [[Ola Bratteli]]<ref>{{cite journal | last=Bratteli | first=Ola | title=Inductive limits of finite dimensional C<sup>*</sup>-algebras | journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society | volume=171 | year=1972 | pages=195&ndash;234 | zbl=0264.46057 | doi=10.1090/s0002-9947-1972-0312282-2| doi-access=free }}</ref> in 1972 in the theory of [[operator algebra]]s to describe directed sequences of finite-dimensional algebras: it played an important role in Elliott's classification of [[approximately finite-dimensional C*-algebra|AF-algebras]] and the theory of [[subfactor]]s.  Subsequently [[Anatoly Vershik]] associated [[dynamical system]]s with infinite paths in such graphs.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Vershik | first=A.M. | authorlink=Anatoly Vershik | title=A theorem on the Markov periodic approximation in ergodic theory | zbl=0559.47006 | journal=Journal of Soviet Mathematics | volume=28 | pages=667–674 | year=1985 | issue=5 | doi=10.1007/bf02112330 | doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Definition==
A Bratteli diagram is given by the following objects:
* A sequence of sets ''V''<sub>''n''</sub> ('the vertices at level ''n''&nbsp;') labeled by positive [[integer]] set '''N'''.  In some literature each element v of ''V''<sub>''n''</sub> is accompanied by a positive integer ''b''<sub>''v''</sub>&nbsp;>&nbsp;0.
* A sequence of sets ''E''<sub>''n''</sub> ('the edges from level ''n'' to ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1&nbsp;') labeled by '''N''', endowed with maps&nbsp;''s'': ''E''<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;→&nbsp;''V''<sub>''n''</sub> and ''r'':&nbsp;''E''<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;→&nbsp;''V''<sub>''n''+1</sub>, such that:
** For each ''v'' in ''V''<sub>''n''</sub>, the number of elements ''e'' in ''E''<sub>''n''</sub> with ''s''(''e'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''v'' is finite.
** So is the number of ''e''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''E''<sub>''n''&minus;1</sub> with ''r''(''e'') =&nbsp;''v''.
** When the vertices have markings by positive integers ''b''<sub>''v''</sub>, the number ''a''<sub>''v'',&nbsp;''v''&nbsp;'</sub> of the edges with ''s''(''e'') =&nbsp;''v'' and ''r''(''e'') = v' for ''v''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''V''<sub>''n''</sub> and v'&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''V''<sub>''n''+1</sub> satisfies ''b''<sub>''v''</sub>&nbsp;''a''<sub>v,&nbsp;v'</sub> ≤&nbsp;''b''<sub>v'</sub>.

A customary way to pictorially represent Bratteli diagrams is to align the vertices according to their levels, and put the number ''b''<sub>''v''</sub> beside the vertex ''v'', or use that number in place of ''v'', as in

[[File:Sample Bratteli diagram.svg|frameless|center|alt=E_0{{=}}{a}. a is labeled 1, and has two edges to b and one to c. E_1{{=}}{b,c}. b is labeled 2, and has one edge to d. c is labeled 1, and has one edge to d and one to e. E_2{{=}}{d,e}. d is labeled 3, and has one edge to f. e is labeled 1, and has one edge to f and one to g. E_3{{=}}{f,g}. f is labeled 4. g is labeled 1.
Etc.]]

An '''ordered Bratteli diagram''' is a Bratteli diagram together with a partial order on ''E''<sub>''n''</sub> such that for any ''v''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''V''<sub>''n''</sub> the set {&nbsp;''e''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''E''<sub>''n''−1</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''r''(''e'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''v''&nbsp;} is totally ordered. Edges that do not share a common range vertex are incomparable. This partial order allows us to define the set of all maximal edges ''E''<sub>max</sub> and the set of all minimal edges ''E''<sub>min</sub>. A Bratteli diagram with a unique infinitely long path in ''E''<sub>max</sub> and ''E''<sub>min</sub> is called ''essentially simple''.
<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Herman |first1=Richard H. |last2=Putnam |first2=Ian F. |last3=Skau |first3=Christian F. |title=Ordered Bratteli diagrams, dimension groups and topological dynamics |journal=International Journal of Mathematics |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=827–864 |year=1992 |doi=10.1142/S0129167X92000382 }}</ref>

==Sequence of finite-dimensional algebras==
Any [[semisimple algebra]] over the [[complex numbers]] '''C''' of finite dimension can be expressed as a [[direct sum of algebras|direct sum]] ⊕<sub>k</sub> M<sub>n<sub>k</sub></sub>('''C''') of [[matrix ring|matrix algebras]], and the '''C'''-algebra homomorphisms between two such algebras up to inner automorphisms on both sides are completely determined by the multiplicity number between 'matrix algebra' components.  Thus, an injective homomorphism of ⊕<sub>''k''=1</sub><sup>''i''</sup>&nbsp;''M''<sub>''n''<sub>''k''</sub></sub>('''C''') into ⊕<sub>''l''=1</sub><sup>''j''</sup>&nbsp;''M''<sub>''m''<sub>''l''</sub></sub>('''C''') may be represented by a collection of positive numbers ''a''<sub>''k'', ''l''</sub> satisfying Σ&nbsp;''n''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;''a''<sub>''k'',&nbsp;l</sub> ≤&nbsp;''m''<sub>''l''</sub>. (The equality holds [[if and only if]] the homomorphism is unital; we can allow non-injective homomorphisms by allowing some ''a''<sub>''k'',''l''</sub> to be zero.)  This can be illustrated as a [[bipartite graph]] having the vertices marked by numbers (''n''<sub>''k''</sub>)<sub>''k''</sub> on one hand and the ones marked by (''m''<sub>''l''</sub>)<sub>''l''</sub> on the other hand, and having ''a''<sub>''k'',&nbsp;''l''</sub> edges between the vertex ''n''<sub>''k''</sub> and the vertex&nbsp;''m''<sub>''l''</sub>.

Thus, when we have a sequence of finite-dimensional semisimple algebras ''A''<sub>''n''</sub> and injective homomorphisms ''φ''<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''A''<sub>''n'''</sub>&nbsp;→&nbsp;''A''<sub>''n''+1</sub>: between them, we obtain a Bratteli diagram by putting

: ''V''<sub>''n''</sub> = the set of simple components of ''A''<sub>''n''</sub>

(each isomorphic to a matrix algebra), marked by the size of matrices.

: (''E''<sub>''n''</sub>, ''r'', ''s''): the number of the edges between ''M''<sub>''n''<sub>''k''</sub></sub>('''C''') ⊂ ''A''<sub>''n''</sub> and ''M''<sub>''m''<sub>''l''</sub></sub>('''C''') ⊂ ''A''<sub>''n''+1</sub> is equal to the multiplicity of ''M''<sub>''n''<sub>''k''</sub></sub>('''C''') into ''M''<sub>''m''<sub>''l''</sub></sub>('''C''') under ''&phi;''<sub>''n''</sub>.

==Sequence of split semisimple algebras==

Any [[semisimple algebra]] (possibly of infinite dimension) is one whose [[Module (mathematics)|modules]] are completely reducible, i.e. they decompose into the direct sum of [[Module (mathematics)#Types of modules|simple modules]]. Let <math> A_0 \subseteq A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \cdots </math> be a chain of split semisimple algebras, and let <math>\hat A_i</math> be the indexing set for the irreducible representations of <math>A_i</math>. Denote by <math>A_i^\lambda</math> the irreducible module indexed by <math>\lambda \in \hat A_i</math>. Because of the inclusion <math>A_i \subseteq A_{i+1}</math>, any <math>A_{i+1}</math>-module <math>M</math> restricts to a <math>A_i</math>-module. Let <math>g_{\lambda, \mu}</math> denote the decomposition numbers

: <math> A_{i+1}^\mu \downarrow^{A_{i+1}}_{A_i} = \bigoplus_{\lambda \in \hat A_i} g_{\lambda,\mu} A_i^\lambda.</math>

The '''Bratteli diagram''' for the chain <math> A_0 \subseteq A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \cdots </math> is obtained by placing one vertex for every element of <math>\hat A_i</math> on level <math>i</math> and connecting a vertex <math>\lambda</math> on level <math>i</math> to a vertex <math>\mu</math> on level <math>i+1</math> with <math>g_{\lambda,\mu}</math> edges.

===Examples===

[[File:Brauer-Bratteli.jpg|thumb|Bratteli diagram for Brauer and BMW algebras on i=0,1,2,3, and 4 strands.]]

(1) If <math>A_i = S_i</math>, the ith [[symmetric group]], the corresponding Bratteli diagram is the same as [[Young's lattice]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Alcock-Zeilinger |first1=Judith M. |title=The Symmetric Group, its Representations, and Combinatorics |url=https://www.math.uni-tuebingen.de/de/forschung/maphy/lehre/ws-2018-19/sgc/dateien/combinatorics-lecturenotes.pdf |website=University of Tübingen Department of Mathematics |at=Th. 4.5}}</ref>

(2) If <math>A_i</math> is the [[Brauer algebra]] or the [[Birman–Wenzl algebra]] on ''i'' strands, then the resulting Bratteli diagram has partitions of ''i''–2''k'' (for <math>k=0,1,2,\ldots,\lfloor i/2 \rfloor</math>) with one edge between partitions on adjacent levels if one can be obtained from the other by adding or subtracting 1 from a single part.

(3) If <math>A_i</math> is the [[Temperley–Lieb algebra]] on ''i'' strands, the resulting Bratteli has integers ''i''–2''k'' (for <math>k=0,1,2,\ldots,\lfloor i/2 \rfloor</math>) with one edge between integers on adjacent levels if one can be obtained from the other by adding or subtracting 1.
